newsitem.title: CONGO: ZAIRE'S MOBUTU BLOCKED FROM TALKS BY 31 STEPS.
newsitem.headline: ZAIRE'S MOBUTU BLOCKED FROM TALKS BY 31 STEPS.

text.p: Zaire's ailing president Mobutu Sese Seko waited in Congo's port of Pointe Noire on Friday -- prevented by 31 steep steps from boarding a South African ship for talks with rebel leader Laurent Kabila.
"The problem is the steep metal steps," said one South African official on the converted ice-breaker SAS Outeniqua, where South African President Nelson Mandela waited to host the meeting.
The 31 steps lead up from the quayside to the ship.
South African and Zairean officials told reporters they were examining the option of building a makeshift ramp so the veteran leader could be driven onto the Outeniqua, moored in Pointe Noire.
Hoisting him on by crane was another option, they added.
Mobutu, 66, has dominated Zaire since seizing power in 1965 but prostate cancer and a whirlwind rebel offensive have weakened his grip on power.
Zairean Foreign Minister Kamanda wa Kamanda told reporters doctors had also advised Mobutu against being flown on board by helicopter because the vibrations would be bad for him.
But Kamanda remained optimistic. "The president is going to come," he told reporters on the Outeniqua, after a delay of well over three hours.
Kamanda said Mobutu, who flew by plane from Kinshasa earlier on Friday and was waiting at the airport of the coastal city of Pointe Noire, was in good spirits.
The Outeniqua was to leave Pointe Noire and sail south for two hours to pick Kabila up off the coast of Angola, where he was waiting in the capital Luanda.
South African Deputy President Thabo Mbeki was also in Angola to escort Kabila on board by helicopter. Mandela was to have brought Mobutu onto the ship, but went ahead alone.
Officials said any talks were due to begin with a face-to-face meeting between the two Zaireans, in the presence of Mandela, followed by a broader meeting with other leaders.
"In my view this meeting will produce a process that involves a transfer of power and hopefully a transitional inclusive government," U.S. envoy Bill Richardson said.
Richardson helped Mandela bring the two civil war foes together. The rebels took up arms in October and control around three-quarters of Zaire.
